title: Cap. 3 Obj. 4: If the death is applicable to all, are resurrection, intercession, and mediation likewise?
pass_a_gloss: Obj.4: if death applicable-to-any, then resurrection/intercession/mediation likewise to all; but Christ not raised/interceding/Mediator for all (Rom 8:34; 4:25) — ergo death not for all. Sol: we deny de-facto applied-to-all and deny infallible-application-by-predestination; affirm lytron by which any sins expiable under Gospel conditions. Gospel herald can announce to any human (not fallen angels) salvation obtainable if believes — so conditional promise rests on Divine ordination regarding humans. Resurrection/intercession/mediation same right as death: to whole race = possibility under faith; to elect = infallibility from destined faith. Special restriction of merits to elect later; yet death/merits of him who assumed all's nature announcible/offerable/applicable by faith to all sharing human nature (John 3:17–18). Non-believers still had life obtainable if they had believed.
pass_b_english: Obj. 4. If Christ's death is to be considered as a remedy or lytron applicable to any human being by God's ordination, then Christ's resurrection, intercession, and mediation will likewise look to all in the same way. But Christ was not raised for all, does not intercede for all, is not the Mediator of all: therefore neither is his death to be extended to all. That these must never be torn apart is proved from ([[Romans 8:34 >> Bible:Romans 8:34]]), where all are joined together: It is Christ who died, yes rather who rose again, who is also at the right hand of the Father, making intercession for us. And ([[Romans 4:25 >> Bible:Romans 4:25]]): the Apostle teaches that for whose offenses Christ died, for their justification he was also raised: but he was not raised for all; therefore neither did he die for all.

Sol. If the reason of our defense is rightly weighed, it will easily appear that all this brings no detriment to our cause. For we do not maintain that Christ's death is, by God's ordination, so applied to all and each human being that on account of this propitiatory sacrifice the whole are immediately set back into a state of grace and salvation; nor do we defend that, from God's special intention and the decree of predestination, this death of Christ is to be applied infallibly to all and each; but that this death, God so ordaining and revealing it in his word, is that lytron by which the sins of any human beings whatsoever can be expiated, the conditions required in the Gospel being fulfilled. And hence it is that the Gospel preacher, whomever he meets under whatever sky, can confidently announce to him salvation obtainable in the death of the Son of God, if he believes. This can be promised to none of the fallen angels. Whence it is clear that this conditional promise of salvation in Christ's death, which can be announced to any human being, is founded in some ordination of the Divine will which regards human beings universally and individually, and does not regard angels. Let the adversaries say what this ordination is, if it is not that which we affirm — of Christ's death as applicable to the human race under the Gospel conditions. These things being so established, we come nearer to the solution of the said objection; and we affirm that Christ's resurrection, intercession, and mediation pertain to all and each by the same right as the death itself, or the oblation accomplished on the cross. For as we can truly announce to any human being that his sins are, by God's ordination, expiable by Christ's death, and will be expiated if only he believes in Christ; so also we can truly announce that the same Christ has been raised that he may justify that believer, exalted to the right hand of God that by his mediation and merits he may preserve that believer in grace with God, and at length lead him to glory. We do not therefore tear apart what God has joined, but teach that Christ's death, resurrection, and intercession are joined by an indissoluble bond — yet in different ways. If we look to the universal human race, that is, to all and each human being, then we say that not only the death but also the resurrection and intercession of Christ look to them as to the possibility of enjoying these benefits, the condition of faith being presupposed: if we look to the elect, we affirm that all these look to them as to the infallibility of enjoying them, from this condition of faith destined for them and to be given them in time. Although therefore in a certain special respect Christ's death and resurrection, with the vast treasure of his merits, are restricted to the elect alone (of which we shall treat later), yet it is not to be denied that the death and merits of Christ, who soundly assumed the nature of all and one cause of all, are of such a kind as can be announced, offered, and applied by faith to all and each who share human nature. Christ himself indicated this clearly enough in ([[John 3:17–18 >> Bible:John 3:17]]) in these words: God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world, but that the world through him might be saved. He that believes on him is not condemned: he that believes not is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God. Those therefore who never believe or will believe nonetheless had life obtainable in the death and merits of Christ by God's ordination, if they had believed.
source_text:
Obj. 4. Si mors Christi consideranda sit tanquam remedium vel lytron ex ordinatione cuivis homini applicabile, tum etiam resurrectio, intercessio, mediatio Christi ad omnes spectabunt eodem modo: At Christus non est excitatus pro omnibus, non intercedit pro omnibus, non est Mediator omnium: Ergo nec mors ejus ad omnes extendenda est. Haec nunquam esse divellenda probatur ex Rom. viii. 34. ubi conjunguntur omnia: Christus est qui mortuus est, imo qui resurrexit, qui etiam est ad dextram Patris, postulans pro nobis. Et Rom. iv. 25. Docet Apostolus, propter quorum offensas mortuus est Christus, propter eorundem justificationem excitatum fuisse: Non est autem excitatus pro omnibus: Ergo nec mortuus.

Sol. Si defensionis nostrae ratio rite perpendatur, facile constabit haec omnia causae nostrae nihil afferre detrimenti. Non enim tuemur mortem Christi esse ex ordinatione Dei ita applicatam omnibus et singulis hominibus, ut propter hoc propitiatorium sacrificium reponantur illico universi in statum gratiae et salutis: neque illud defendimus, ex speciali intentione Dei et praedestinationis decreto hanc mortem Christi esse infallibiliter omnibus et singulis applicandam; sed hanc mortem, Deo ita ordinante et in verbo suo revelante, esse illud lytron, quo expiari possunt peccata quorumcunque hominum, praestitis conditionibus in Evangelio requisitis. Atque hinc est quod praeco Evangelicus, quemcunque hominem convenerit sub quacunque coeli plaga, potest confidenter illi annunciare in morte Filii Dei salutem parabilem, si crediderit. Hoc nulli angelorum lapsorum promitti potest. Unde clarum est, hanc conditionalem promissionem salutis in morte Christi, quae annunciari potest cuivis homini, fundatam esse in aliqua ordinatione voluntatis Divinae, quae homines universim et sigillatim spectat, angelos non spectat. Dicant autem adversarii quae haec sit ordinatio, si non sit illa quam nos afferimus, de morte Christi humano generi sub conditionibus Evangelicis applicabili. Hisce ita constitutis propius accedimus ad dictae objectionis solutionem; et affirmamus, pari jure resurrectionem, intercessionem et mediationem Christi ad omnes et singulos pertinere quo mors ipsa sive oblatio in cruce peracta. Nam ut vere cuivis homini annunciare possumus peccata ejus morte Christi esse ex ordinatione Dei expiabilia, et fore expiata, si modo crediderit in Christum; ita et vere annunciare possumus eundem Christum resuscitatum esse ut illum credentem justificet, exaltatum ad dextram Dei ut sua mediatione et meritis illum credentem in gratia apud Deum conservet, et tandem ad gloriam perducat. Non itaque ea divellimus quae Deus conjunxit, sed mortem, resurrectionem et intercessionem Christi nexu indissolubili conjunctas docemus, at diversimode. Si spectemus humanum genus universum, hoc est, omnes et singulos homines, tum dicimus, non modo mortem sed resurrectionem et intercessionem Christi ad illos spectare quoad possibilitatem fruendi hisce beneficiis, praesupposita fidei conditione: Si spectemus electos, affirmamus haec omnia ad eos spectare quoad infallibilitatem fruendi, ex destinata scilicet et in tempore illis donanda hac fidei conditione. Quamvis ergo speciali quadam ratione mors et resurrectio Christi, cum ingenti thesauro meritorum ejus, ad solos electos restringatur, (de quo postea disseremus) tamen non est negandum mortem ac merita Christi, qui sanus omnium naturam et unam omnium causam suscepit, esse ejusmodi quae possunt omnibus et singulis humanam naturam participantibus annunciari, offerri et per fidem applicari. Hoc ipse Christus satis clare indicavit, Johann. iii. 17, 18. hisce verbis, Non misit Deus Filium suum in mundum ut condemnet mundum, sed ut servetur mundus per eum. Qui credit in eum non condemnabitur: qui non credit jam condemnatus est, quia non credidit in nomen unigeniti Filii Dei. Illi igitur qui nunquam credunt aut credituri sunt, habuerunt tamen vitam in morte meritisque Christi ex ordinatione Dei parabilem, si credidissent.
